transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Well, I suppose it's because of what happened at the restaurant. I mean, I didn't think it was that big of a deal at first, but my manager insisted I come see someone. I've been waitressing for years, you know? It's usually second nature to me, the flow of it all, carrying the trays, remembering who had the side salad and who wanted extra ranch. But lately... well, what scared everyone at work is that I started freezing up in the middle of service. Just... stopping. Or I'd start doing things completely out of order. Like, the other day, during the lunch rush—which is always crazy, right?—I found myself just standing by the soda station. I was holding the cash drawer key, which I wasn't even supposed to have right then, and I was just repeating table numbers out loud. "Table four, table seven, table nine..." just over and over, instead of actually closing out the checks like I was supposed to be doing. And I couldn't seem to snap out of it right away. My coworker, Sarah, she had to physically tap me on the shoulder to get me to move. She said I looked like a statue. It's just... it's really embarrassing, honestly, and it's making everyone nervous.
During these freezing spells, are you aware of what’s happening around you?

Am I aware? I mean... it's hard to say, really. Because, well, you'd think I'd know, right? You'd think if you're standing in the middle of a busy restaurant, with the clinking of the silverware and the kitchen bell ringing—our line cook, Tony, is always ringing that bell, it's so loud, he hits it like three times for every single order just to rush us—you'd think I'd be completely aware of all that noise and chaos. But when I freeze like that... I don't know, I'm really not sure what I'm processing. 

It's almost like I'm there, but I'm not *there*. I don't remember seeing Sarah actually walk up to me. I just remember the sudden feeling of her hand on my shoulder, and it startled me, almost like waking up from a nap you didn't know you were taking. But I wasn't asleep, obviously, I was standing right there by the soda machine, holding that cash drawer key. So I guess... I really don't know if I'm aware of my surroundings or not. It's not like I'm passed out on the floor, but I'm definitely not paying attention to the lunch rush either, which is just so weird for me because I'm usually the one keeping everyone else on track, you know? Like, I'm the one who always remembers that the regulars at table four need extra lemons for their iced tea, and I never drop the ball on that. But during those moments, it's just... I couldn't tell you what was happening right in front of my face.
After one of these freezing spells ends, are there parts of what happened during it that you can’t remember?

I mean, I don't think I'm actually forgetting anything, really. It's not like I have amnesia or anything dramatic like you see in those soap operas my mom watches—she's obsessed with them, always has them on in the background, and someone's always getting hit on the head and forgetting their whole life. It's definitely not like that. It's more just... well, like I said, I'm not really sure what I'm taking in during those moments anyway. So it's not that I can't remember what happened, it's more like I wasn't really recording it in the first place, if that makes sense? 

Like, if you asked me what Tony the cook was yelling about while I was standing by the soda machine, I couldn't tell you. But I don't think I *forgot* what he was yelling, I just don't think I heard it at all while I was stuck like that. Because usually, I remember everything. I have to! In my job, if you forget that the guy at table six wanted his dressing on the side, he'll send the whole salad back and then the kitchen gets backed up, and Tony starts slamming pans around, and it throws off the whole rhythm of the shift. I'm usually so sharp with my memory. I can remember orders from regulars who haven't been in for months. But with these... these freezing things... I don't feel like I'm losing memories. I just feel like there's a gap where I wasn't really paying attention to anything except whatever table numbers I was mumbling. So, no, I wouldn't say I can't remember parts of it, because there isn't really anything *to* remember from my end, you know? Just... blank space until Sarah touches my shoulder.
After one of these spells ends, do you feel confused?

Confused? Well, I wouldn't really use the word confused. I mean, when I think of being confused, I think of, you know, when they change the menu on us without telling us—which management actually did last month, they swapped out the seasonal vegetables and completely changed the POS system layout overnight. *That* was confusing. Everyone was running around trying to figure out where the button for the sweet potato fries went. But after these... these spells... it's not like that. 

It's more just... jarring, I guess? Like I said, when Sarah touched my shoulder, I jumped. It was like I was suddenly just *back*. I knew exactly where I was, I knew I was at the restaurant, I knew I was holding the cash drawer key—even though I still don't know why I grabbed it in the first place—and I knew it was the lunch rush. I wasn't disoriented about my surroundings or who I was or anything like that. I just felt... embarrassed, mostly. And maybe a little frustrated, because I knew I was holding up the line and I had tables waiting. So, no, I don't feel confused like my brain is scrambled. I just feel like I was paused, and then someone hit play again, and I just have to catch up to the speed everyone else is already moving at. But I know exactly what I'm supposed to be doing once I'm back. I just get right back to it, or try to, anyway, once the embarrassment wears off a little.
Right before one of these spells starts, do you notice a strange warning feeling?

A warning feeling? Hmm. No, I don't think so. I mean, it's not like I get a headache first, or my vision goes blurry, or anything like that. You know how some people say they can feel a thunderstorm coming because their knees ache? My aunt used to say that all the time, she'd sit on the porch and say, "It's gonna pour, my left knee is acting up," and sure enough, twenty minutes later, it would be raining. It's definitely not like that. There's no physical sign or... or weird feeling that tells me it's about to happen. 

It's really just... sudden. One second I'm walking toward the back station to grab extra napkins for table nine—because table nine always asks for extra napkins, it's a family with three little kids and they make such a mess, but they tip well so I don't mind—and the next thing I know, I'm just stuck there, mumbling numbers. I don't feel a shift in my mood, I don't feel dizzy, I don't feel like the room is spinning. I'm just doing my job, going about my shift, trying to keep up with the lunch rush, and then... bam. I'm paused. So, no, I wouldn't say there's any kind of strange warning or premonition or whatever you want to call it. It just sort of sneaks up on me, which honestly makes it even more frustrating because I can't prepare for it or tell someone to cover my section for a minute. It just happens right in the middle of whatever I'm doing.
During these spells, do you ever make repetitive movements without meaning to, like lip smacking, chewing, fumbling with your hands, or picking at things?

Repetitive movements? Like... like chewing or picking at things? No, no, definitely not. I mean, I'm already stuck there like a statue, right? It's not like I'm doing a whole routine. I'm just frozen. 

Except for the mumbling, of course, which I already told you about. The table numbers. But my hands? No, they just stay wherever they were. Like when I had that cash drawer key—my hand was just clamped around it. I wasn't fumbling with it or tossing it up in the air or anything. And I definitely wasn't smacking my lips or chewing. I mean, can you imagine? Standing in the middle of a busy restaurant, staring into space, mumbling numbers, and smacking my lips like I'm eating invisible food? It's embarrassing enough just freezing. If I was doing all that extra stuff, Tony would probably throw a spatula at me. 

So, no, my body is just... still. Rigid, almost. It's not like when my cousin gets nervous—she has this awful habit where she picks at her cuticles until they bleed. She does it without even realizing it, especially when we're watching a tense movie or something. I always have to swat her hand away. But this isn't like a nervous habit or a fidget. I'm not fidgeting at all. I'm just completely stopped in my tracks. Like, if I'm holding a tray, the tray just stays there. I'm not tapping my fingers on it or adjusting my grip. It's just... nothing. Just the freezing and the mumbling.
During one of these spells, have you ever fallen down or had shaking of your body?

Fallen down? Or shaking? Oh, gosh, no. No, thank goodness. I mean, can you imagine? The floors at the restaurant are already such a hazard on a normal day. They mop them, sure, but they use this cheap, greasy cleaner, and even with those mandatory non-slip black shoes we have to wear—which, by the way, are incredibly uncomfortable, they have absolutely zero arch support and my feet are just screaming by the end of a double shift—people slip and fall all the time. Just last week, one of the bussers went down hard near the dish pit. But during these spells of mine? No, I stay right on my feet. I don't collapse, I don't faint, I don't even lose my balance. If I did, I would have definitely ended up in the hospital by now, because falling in that dining room means you're probably taking a tray of hot soup or a stack of heavy ceramic plates down with you, and that would be a total disaster. 

And shaking? No, definitely not shaking either. Like I was trying to explain a minute ago, I'm just completely still. Like a statue. If I was shaking or trembling, I'd probably drop whatever I was holding. My aunt has this little dog, a tiny Chihuahua mix, and he shakes all over whenever there's a thunderstorm or a loud noise, just his whole body vibrating. It's nothing like that. My body doesn't jerk around or shiver or anything. I just... lock up. I stand there perfectly upright, completely frozen, not moving a single muscle except for my mouth doing that mumbling thing with the numbers. So, yeah, no falling, no shaking, just... standing there stuck in place.
After one of these spells ends, do you feel unusually sleepy?

Sleepy? Um, well. I mean, I'm a waitress working double shifts, so I'm pretty much always some level of tired, you know? It's just the nature of the job. You're on your feet all day, running back and forth from the kitchen to the floor, dealing with demanding customers, carrying those heavy trays... by the time I clock out, I'm completely exhausted. 

But unusually sleepy right after one of those freezing spells? No, not really. It's not like I suddenly need to take a nap or anything like that. When it ends, it's just... over. Like somebody finally hit the play button again. I just blink, realize I've been standing there stuck, and then I just have to jump right back into whatever I was doing because, like I said, the lunch rush doesn't wait for anybody. If I got sleepy every time it happened, I wouldn't even make it through my shift. I'd be trying to doze off in the breakroom. And you really can't do that at my restaurant anyway. The breakroom is ridiculously tiny, it barely fits two chairs, and the ice machine is right next to the wall and it is so loud it sounds like an airplane taking off every time it cycles, so nobody really rests in there even if they wanted to. 

So, yeah, back to your question, no sudden exhaustion or sleepiness. I might feel a little flustered or, I don't know, annoyed that it happened again, especially if I think Tony or one of the other servers noticed me just standing there staring into space. But physically? I'm totally awake. My energy level doesn't just drop off a cliff. I just pick up my tray or my notepad, take a breath, and keep moving. So no, no weird sleepiness. Just the regular, everyday exhaustion of the job.
About how long does each freezing spell usually last?

How long do they last? Well, it's hard to say exactly, because when I'm in it, time sort of... I don't know, it feels different. But it's long enough. It's long enough that people notice, and that's the part that really scares everyone at work. I mean, it's not just a quick second where I zone out. It's a whole thing. 

Like, what really freaked everyone out was when I started freezing up right in the middle of a busy service. I'd just be standing there, completely locked up. Or I'd start doing things completely out of order. There was this one time, and this is what really got Tony on my case, I was standing over by the soda station—which is always a chaotic mess anyway, because the Diet Coke syrup is always running out and nobody ever changes the box—and I was just standing there, holding the key to the cash drawer. I was supposed to be closing out checks for my section, right? Because table 12 was waiting to leave and they had theatre tickets. But instead of going to the register, I'm just standing by the soda fountain, clutching this key, and repeating table numbers over and over. "Table 4, table 7, table 12..." Just mumbling them. 

And I was stuck like that for... I don't know, it felt like forever, but Tony said it was a good couple of minutes. Two or three minutes of just standing there, holding a key I wasn't using, not closing the checks, just repeating numbers while the ice machine is roaring next to me. So it's long enough to completely derail what I'm doing and make everyone stare at me like I've lost my mind. It's just so embarrassing, you know? Because I know I have a job to do, and I'm a good waitress, I really am, I can balance four plates on one arm, but when I get stuck like that, I just... I can't do anything until it passes.
Do these freezing spells tend to happen when you’re feeling especially stressed or emotionally upset?

Stressed? Emotionally upset? Well, I mean, working in a restaurant is basically one long, continuous state of stress, if we're being completely honest. You've got the kitchen line cooks yelling that food is dying in the window, customers waving you down because they urgently need a side of ranch dressing or a mountain of extra lemons for their water, and the managers are always breathing down your neck about table turnover times. It's a total pressure cooker. I've been doing this a long time, ever since I took a break from college, so I'm usually pretty used to the rush, but it definitely gets to you. 

So, when you ask if it happens when I'm stressed... I guess the answer is yes, because, like I was literally just telling you a second ago about that whole incident with the cash drawer key? That happened right in the absolute thick of the lunch rush. That's exactly what scared everyone at work so badly. It wasn't just that I froze up, it's that I started freezing up right in the middle of service and doing things completely out of order right when we were getting slammed. 

Like I said, Table 12 was practically having a panic attack because they were going to be late for their theatre tickets, and I was supposed to be closing their check. That's a lot of pressure! But instead of doing the normal sequence—you know, take the card, go to the POS system, run the card, bring back the receipt—the stress just... I don't know, it just scrambled everything. I ended up all the way over by the soda station. Just standing there, clutching that register key, completely ignoring the checks I was supposed to be
During these freezing spells, can you hear people talking to you?

Hear people? Um, well, yes and no. It's... it's complicated. I mean, it's not like my ears stop working, right? The physical ability to hear is still there. Like I mentioned before, the ice machine by the soda station is practically deafening, and I can definitely hear that roar when I'm stuck there. But as for people talking to me... it's like their voices are coming through a thick pane of glass, or like I'm underwater. 

I know they're talking. I can hear the sound of Tony's voice, and usually he's sounding pretty frantic or annoyed because, like I keep saying, this always seems to happen when we're in the weeds. But it's like my brain just can't process what the words actually mean. I'm stuck in that loop. Like that time I was telling you about, when I was just standing there by the soda fountain clutching the cash drawer key? Tony was right there, probably shouting my name, asking me what on earth I was doing, because I was supposed to be closing out Table 12 so they could get to their play. 

I was doing everything completely out of order, just standing there repeating, "Table 4, table 7, table 12," over and over. I could hear the noise of the restaurant, the clinking plates, the kitchen bell dinging, Tony's voice... but I couldn't respond. I couldn't break out of the freezing or the mumbling to actually answer him or do what I was supposed to do. It's like my body and my mouth are just doing their own thing, completely disconnected from the instructions people are giving me. So, yes, the sound gets in, but the meaning? The meaning just completely bounces off. It's incredibly frustrating, honestly, because I know I look completely ridiculous just standing there holding a key I'm not using while people are talking right at me.
When someone touches you or calls your name during one of these spells, can you stop it right away?

Stop it right away? Oh, I wish. I really, really wish I could. Because if I could just snap out of it the second someone said my name or tapped my shoulder, I wouldn't be in half the trouble I'm in with management right now. But no, it doesn’t work like that at all. 

Like, if Tony comes up and grabs my arm... and he has, he actually did exactly that during that same lunch rush I just keep talking about. Because, like I was telling you, what really scared everyone at work is that I started freezing up right in the absolute middle of service, just completely doing things out of order. So when I was standing over by the soda station—you know, holding that cash drawer key and just repeating those table numbers over and over instead of actually going to the POS system and closing out the checks like I was supposed to—Tony came over and he actually grabbed my shoulder. Not meanly, just, you know, trying to physically shake me out of it, saying my name really loud right in my ear. 

But even with him touching me, even with him right in my face trying to break the spell, I just... I couldn't stop. I couldn't just drop the key and go to the register. It's like my brain was still completely stuck on 'Table 4, table 7, table 12' and my body just wouldn't listen to the fact that someone was physically shaking me. It takes a while for it to wear off, for the gears to finally catch again, I guess you could say. And until they do, it really doesn't matter who touches me or how loud they yell my name. I'm just stuck there doing the wrong thing in the wrong place, and I just have to wait for it to end. It makes me feel so helpless, honestly, because I can feel his hand on my shoulder, but I just can't make myself snap out of it.
During these spells, do people say you have a blank stare?

A blank stare? Yeah, I mean... that's exactly what they said. That's the part that really freaked Tony out, I think. Because, like I've been saying, what really scared everyone at work is that I started freezing up right in the absolute middle of service, just right in the thick of it. And doing things completely out of order. 

I mean, I'm standing there by the soda station, right? And I've got the cash drawer key clutched in my hand, and I'm supposed to be closing out these checks—especially Table 12, who are practically having a heart attack about their theatre tickets—and instead I'm just standing there, repeating, "Table 4, table 7, table 12," over and over again. And Tony said that when he came over and grabbed my shoulder, he looked right into my eyes, and he said nobody was home. He said I was just staring straight through the soda machine, like my eyes were totally glazed over and completely blank. 

He told me later, when we were sitting in the break room and I was trying to stop crying, he said it was like looking at a mannequin. That's the word he used—mannequin. Because I wasn't blinking, I wasn't looking at him, I wasn't looking at the key in my hand or the receipts I was supposed to be handling... I was just staring off into absolute nothingness while my mouth just kept mumbling those table numbers. It's embarrassing, really. Just thinking about looking like that, totally checked out with this dead-eyed stare while the whole restaurant is falling apart around me... it's just really hard to hear that about yourself, you know?
Have you ever had an EEG that showed seizure activity?

An EEG? Um, you mean the... the test with the little sticky wires they put all over your head? No, no I haven't had anything like that done. I mean, honestly, I haven't really been to a lot of doctors for this until now. Because, you know, working in the service industry, the health insurance isn't exactly stellar, and taking time off to go get a bunch of expensive tests done just isn't something I can easily do. Especially when we're so short-staffed and I'm already in hot water with management over these freezing spells. 

Tony actually made me go to the urgent care after that really bad shift I keep telling you about—the one where I was stuck by the soda machine with the cash drawer key just repeating those table numbers while Table 12 was waiting to pay—but all they did there was take my blood pressure, shine a light in my eyes, and tell me I seemed stressed out. They definitely didn't hook my brain up to any machines or do any major scans. 

And as for seizures... I mean, I always thought a seizure was when you fall on the floor and shake, right? Like what you see on medical shows? I wasn't doing anything like that at all. I was just standing perfectly still, like Tony said, like a mannequin. Just totally frozen and mumbling. So, no, nobody has ever mentioned seizures to me before, and I definitely haven't had an EEG or any kind of test that would show something like that.
Have any of these spells ever happened when you were completely alone?

When I'm completely alone? You know, I've actually spent a lot of time thinking about that exact question since this all started. Because, I mean, if I'm just in my apartment, right? Just trying to fold my laundry or watching TV or something, and I happen to have one of these spells... how would I even really know? 

There's no Tony there to shake my shoulder, there's no customers staring at me. I might just think I got lost in thought for a few minutes, or got distracted, you know? So it's entirely possible that it happens when I'm by myself in my living room, but I just don't have the audience to point it out to me. 

But honestly, whether it happens when I'm alone or not almost feels beside the point to me right now, because the reason I'm sitting here talking to you—and I know I sound like a total broken record bringing up this same lunch shift again, I really do apologize, it's just the one that really brought everything to a head—is what happens when I'm *not* alone. 

Because what really scared everyone at work wasn't me just zoning out in the back alley by myself. It was the fact that I started freezing up right in the absolute middle of service. It's the doing things completely out of order that really freaked people out, I think. Like I said, standing over by the soda station, clutching that cash drawer key for dear life, and just repeating those table numbers over and over instead of actually closing out the checks. If I was alone in my own kitchen mumbling numbers and holding a key, who cares, right? It wouldn't matter. But doing it right out in the open, completely out of order with what I was actually supposed to be doing while the whole restaurant is falling apart... that's why it's a huge problem. So I guess I don't really know for sure about when I'm completely alone, but the public ones are definitely the ones ruining my life right now.
Has anyone ever told you that, during one of these spells, you don’t respond at all when they speak to you?

Yeah, um, they did say that. That's exactly what Tony was saying when we were in the break room. He said he was practically yelling my name, like, right in my ear, and I just... I didn't even flinch. I didn't turn my head, I didn't blink, I just kept staring straight ahead. 

And that's the thing, you know? That's what I keep coming back to. Because if I just, like, dropped a tray or forgot an order, that's one thing. People get stressed, they make mistakes. But this... this is why I'm here. Because what scared everyone at work is that I started freezing up in the absolute middle of service. Just totally unresponsive. And doing things completely out of order, which is just... it's so unlike me. I've been a waitress for years, I know how to handle a rush. 

But there I was, like I mentioned before, just standing by the soda station. And I'm holding the cash drawer key—which I shouldn't even have had at that exact moment because I hadn't printed the receipts yet—and I'm just repeating those table numbers. "Table 4, table 7, table 12." Over and over. Instead of actually closing out the checks like I was supposed to be doing. And Tony is standing right there, asking me what's wrong, telling me Table 12 needs to leave, and I'm just... nothing. No response at all. Just mumbling numbers to the soda machine while holding a key I didn't need yet. It's just so bizarre, and it really freaked everyone out because it's so... it's just so out of order and weird.
During these spells, are you completely unable to respond when someone speaks to you?

Exactly, yeah. I literally cannot get a single word out to answer them. It's not that I'm ignoring anybody, or being rude, it's like my brain just completely disconnects from my mouth. 

And I know I keep bringing up this exact same scenario with the soda machine—I'm sorry, I know I'm probably talking your ear off about it, I must sound crazy just looping back to it—but it just perfectly describes how trapped I feel. Because it's not just that I can't speak to Tony when he's standing there asking me what's wrong, it's that I'm stuck doing these totally nonsensical things and I can't even stop to explain myself. 

That's what really scared everyone at work, honestly. It’s the fact that I started freezing up right in the middle of a busy service while doing things completely out of order. Like I said before, I was standing there clutching the cash drawer key, just repeating the table numbers to myself over and over instead of actually going to the terminal and closing out the checks. Any waitress will tell you that makes absolutely zero sense. You don't grab the register key until the receipts are printed and you have the customer's payment in your hand, but my brain was just... stuck on the wrong step. I was doing it all backwards. And while I'm doing this totally out-of-order stuff, holding a key I don't need, I can't even respond to tell anyone what's happening. I'm just completely locked in, unable to say a single word back to them.
Did these freezing spells start after a head injury?

No, no, I've never hit my head or anything like that. I mean, I've bumped it on a cabinet door once or twice, you know how that goes, but nothing serious. No concussions, no car accidents where I whacked my head on the steering wheel, nothing like that at all. 

And that's what makes this whole thing so frustrating, honestly. Because if I had fallen off a ladder or been in a wreck, at least there would be a reason, right? Like, "Oh, she hit her head, so now she's freezing up and doing things backwards." That would make sense. People would understand that. But this? This just came completely out of nowhere. 

And I know I keep going back to it, but it's just... it's the perfect example of how out of nowhere it is. Because one minute I'm totally fine, handling a lunch rush like I have a hundred times before, and the next minute... it's what scared everyone at work. That I started freezing up in the absolute middle of service, doing things completely out of order. Standing by the soda station, holding that cash drawer key like it's a lifeline, and just repeating those table numbers over and over instead of actually closing out the checks. It's just so backward. And without a head injury or something to blame it on, it just feels like my brain is glitching out for absolutely no reason at all.
Did these freezing spells start after any serious illness, infection, or other medical problem?

No, honestly, I haven't been sick at all. Not even a cold, or a sinus infection, or the flu... nothing like that. I'm actually a really healthy person. I rarely ever call out of work. Usually, I'm the one picking up extra shifts when other people get sick, you know? So there was no fever, no weird virus, no hospital stays... absolutely nothing wrong with me physically. 

And I guess... I know I'm a broken record here, but that just brings me right back to what I was saying before. Because it's just so frustrating not having a physical reason for it. If I had been sick, if I had some crazy high fever that was making me delirious or something, then Tony and the manager would have just been like, "Oh, she's really ill, she needs to go home and rest." But I wasn't sick. I felt totally fine that day. I had my morning coffee, I drove to work, I was taking orders perfectly fine for the first half of my shift. 

And then, just... out of nowhere. I wasn't sick when I was standing by that soda machine. I didn't have an infection when I was clutching that register key and just staring blankly, repeating those table numbers instead of actually printing the receipts. Like I said, what really scared everyone at work is that I started freezing up in the absolute middle of service, doing things completely out of order, and I was physically one hundred percent healthy when it happened. Which just makes it so much scarier, honestly, because there's just no logical medical reason for why my brain would just... stop working like that, and leave me totally trapped and unable to answer anybody.
Right before one of these freezing spells starts, do you suddenly feel intense fear or panic?

No, not before. I mean, I don't get like a sudden wave of terror or a panic attack or anything like that leading up to it. Honestly, right before it happens, I feel completely normal. Just... totally ordinary. There's no warning sign at all, no racing heart, no feeling like something terrible is about to happen, nothing like that. 

Like I was saying, I could just be walking past the expo line, or grabbing a stack of extra napkins, or heading over to the soda station. I'm literally just doing my job, probably thinking about grabbing a side of ranch for table four or wondering if the kitchen is running behind on appetizers, and then... bam. It just hits me. 

The fear doesn't actually come until *after* I'm already stuck. That's when I start panicking, because I realize I'm standing there, holding that stupid register key, and I can't move or speak. It's the feeling of being trapped that's scary, not anything before it. Like when Tony was looking right at me, asking me what was wrong—that's when I felt terrified. Because inside my head I'm screaming, "just answer him, just tell him you're fine, put the key down," but my body is just completely frozen and my brain is just looping on those table numbers instead of doing what it's supposed to do. 

It's so frustrating because if I did feel some kind of intense panic beforehand, maybe I could at least excuse myself, you know? I could run to the breakroom or hide in the employee bathroom. I could tell my manager, "Hey, I feel a panic attack coming on, let me just step off the floor for a second." But because there is absolutely zero fear, zero warning whatsoever before it starts, I just get caught right out in the open. Right in the absolute middle of a busy lunch rush, looking completely out of my mind in front of my coworkers.

patient.answer: Well, I suppose it's because of what happened at the restaurant. I mean, I didn't think it was that big of a deal at first, but my manager insisted I come see someone. I've been waitressing for years, you know? It's usually second nature to me, the flow of it all, carrying the trays, remembering who had the side salad and who wanted extra ranch. But lately... well, what scared everyone at work is that I started freezing up in the middle of service. Just... stopping. Or I'd start doing things completely out of order. Like, the other day, during the lunch rush—which is always crazy, right?—I found myself just standing by the soda station. I was holding the cash drawer key, which I wasn't even supposed to have right then, and I was just repeating table numbers out loud. "Table four, table seven, table nine..." just over and over, instead of actually closing out the checks like I was supposed to be doing. And I couldn't seem to snap out of it right away. My coworker, Sarah, she had to physically tap me on the shoulder to get me to move. She said I looked like a statue. It's just... it's really embarrassing, honestly, and it's making everyone nervous.

patient.answer:
Am I aware? I mean... it's hard to say, really. Because, well, you'd think I'd know, right? You'd think if you're standing in the middle of a busy restaurant, with the clinking of the silverware and the kitchen bell ringing—our line cook, Tony, is always ringing that bell, it's so loud, he hits it like three times for every single order just to rush us—you'd think I'd be completely aware of all that noise and chaos. But when I freeze like that... I don't know, I'm really not sure what I'm processing. 

It's almost like I'm there, but I'm not *there*. I don't remember seeing Sarah actually walk up to me. I just remember the sudden feeling of her hand on my shoulder, and it startled me, almost like waking up from a nap you didn't know you were taking. But I wasn't asleep, obviously, I was standing right there by the soda machine, holding that cash drawer key. So I guess... I really don't know if I'm aware of my surroundings or not. It's not like I'm passed out on the floor, but I'm definitely not paying attention to the lunch rush either, which is just so weird for me because I'm usually the one keeping everyone else on track, you know? Like, I'm the one who always remembers that the regulars at table four need extra lemons for their iced tea, and I never drop the ball on that. But during those moments, it's just... I couldn't tell you what was happening right in front of my face.

patient.answer:
Confused? Well, I wouldn't really use the word confused. I mean, when I think of being confused, I think of, you know, when they change the menu on us without telling us—which management actually did last month, they swapped out the seasonal vegetables and completely changed the POS system layout overnight. *That* was confusing. Everyone was running around trying to figure out where the button for the sweet potato fries went. But after these... these spells... it's not like that. 

It's more just... jarring, I guess? Like I said, when Sarah touched my shoulder, I jumped. It was like I was suddenly just *back*. I knew exactly where I was, I knew I was at the restaurant, I knew I was holding the cash drawer key—even though I still don't know why I grabbed it in the first place—and I knew it was the lunch rush. I wasn't disoriented about my surroundings or who I was or anything like that. I just felt... embarrassed, mostly. And maybe a little frustrated, because I knew I was holding up the line and I had tables waiting. So, no, I don't feel confused like my brain is scrambled. I just feel like I was paused, and then someone hit play again, and I just have to catch up to the speed everyone else is already moving at. But I know exactly what I'm supposed to be doing once I'm back. I just get right back to it, or try to, anyway, once the embarrassment wears off a little.

patient.answer:
A warning feeling? Hmm. No, I don't think so. I mean, it's not like I get a headache first, or my vision goes blurry, or anything like that. You know how some people say they can feel a thunderstorm coming because their knees ache? My aunt used to say that all the time, she'd sit on the porch and say, "It's gonna pour, my left knee is acting up," and sure enough, twenty minutes later, it would be raining. It's definitely not like that. There's no physical sign or... or weird feeling that tells me it's about to happen. 

It's really just... sudden. One second I'm walking toward the back station to grab extra napkins for table nine—because table nine always asks for extra napkins, it's a family with three little kids and they make such a mess, but they tip well so I don't mind—and the next thing I know, I'm just stuck there, mumbling numbers. I don't feel a shift in my mood, I don't feel dizzy, I don't feel like the room is spinning. I'm just doing my job, going about my shift, trying to keep up with the lunch rush, and then... bam. I'm paused. So, no, I wouldn't say there's any kind of strange warning or premonition or whatever you want to call it. It just sort of sneaks up on me, which honestly makes it even more frustrating because I can't prepare for it or tell someone to cover my section for a minute. It just happens right in the middle of whatever I'm doing.

Repetitive movements? Like... like chewing or picking at things? No, no, definitely not. I mean, I'm already stuck there like a statue, right? It's not like I'm doing a whole routine. I'm just frozen.

Like when I had that cash drawer key—my hand was just clamped around it. I wasn't fumbling with it or tossing it up in the air or anything. And I definitely wasn't smacking my lips or chewing. So, no, my body is just... still. Rigid, almost. It's not like when my cousin gets nervous—she has this awful habit where she picks at her cuticles until they bleed. She does it without even realizing it, especially when we're watching a tense movie or something. I always have to swat her hand away. But this isn't like a nervous habit or a fidget. I'm not fidgeting at all. I'm just completely stopped in my tracks. Like, if I'm holding a tray, the tray just stays there. I'm not tapping my fingers on it or adjusting my grip. patient.answer:
Fallen down? Or shaking? Oh, gosh, no. No, thank goodness. I mean, can you imagine? The floors at the restaurant are already such a hazard on a normal day. They mop them, sure, but they use this cheap, greasy cleaner, and even with those mandatory non-slip black shoes we have to wear—which, by the way, are incredibly uncomfortable, they have absolutely zero arch support and my feet are just screaming by the end of a double shift—people slip and fall all the time. Just last week, one of the bussers went down hard near the dish pit. But during these spells of mine? No, I stay right on my feet. I don't collapse, I don't faint, I don't even lose my balance. If I did, I would have definitely ended up in the hospital by now, because falling in that dining room means you're probably taking a tray of hot soup or a stack of heavy ceramic plates down with you, and that would be a total disaster. 

And shaking? No, definitely not shaking either. Like I was trying to explain a minute ago, I'm just completely still. Like a statue. If I was shaking or trembling, I'd probably drop whatever I was holding. My aunt has this little dog, a tiny Chihuahua mix, and he shakes all over whenever there's a thunderstorm or a loud noise, just his whole body vibrating. It's nothing like that. My body doesn't jerk around or shiver or anything. I just... lock up. I stand there perfectly upright, completely frozen, not moving a single muscle except for my mouth doing that mumbling thing with the numbers. So, yeah, no falling, no shaking, just... standing there stuck in place.

So, yeah, back to your question, no sudden exhaustion or sleepiness. But honestly, whether it happens when I'm alone or not almost feels beside the point to me right now, because the reason I'm sitting here talking to you—and I know I sound like a total broken record bringing up this same lunch shift again, I really do apologize, it's just the one that really brought everything to a head—is what happens when I'm *not* alone. 

Because what really scared everyone at work wasn't me just zoning out in the back alley by myself. It was the fact that I started freezing up right in the absolute middle of service. If I was alone in my own kitchen mumbling numbers and holding a key, who cares, right? It wouldn't matter. But doing it right out in the open, completely out of order with what I was actually supposed to be doing while the whole restaurant is falling apart... that's why it's a huge problem. So I guess I don't really know for sure about when I'm completely alone, but the public ones are definitely the ones ruining my life right now.

doctor.intent: Determine whether these episodes are preceded by intense fear or panic, to distinguish epileptic spells from dissociative or other stress-related episodes.

patient.answer:
No, not before. I mean, I don't get like a sudden wave of terror or a panic attack or anything like that leading up to it. Honestly, right before it happens, I feel completely normal. Just... totally ordinary. There's no warning sign at all, no racing heart, no feeling like something terrible is about to happen, nothing like that. 

Like I was saying, I could just be walking past the expo line, or grabbing a stack of extra napkins, or heading over to the soda station. I'm literally just doing my job, probably thinking about grabbing a side of ranch for table four or wondering if the kitchen is running behind on appetizers, and then... bam. It just hits me. 

The fear doesn't actually come until *after* I'm already stuck. That's when I start panicking, because I realize I'm standing there, holding that stupid register key, and I can't move or speak. It's the feeling of being trapped that's scary, not anything before it. Like when Tony was looking right at me, asking me what was wrong—that's when I felt terrified. Because inside my head I'm screaming, "just answer him, just tell him you're fine, put the key down," but my body is just completely frozen and my brain is just looping on those table numbers instead of doing what it's supposed to do. 

It's so frustrating because if I did feel some kind of intense panic beforehand, maybe I could at least excuse myself, you know? I could run to the breakroom or hide in the employee bathroom. I could tell my manager, "Hey, I feel a panic attack coming on, let me just step off the floor for a second." But because there is absolutely zero fear, zero warning whatsoever before it starts, I just get caught right out in the open. Right in the absolute middle of a busy lunch rush, looking completely out of my mind in front of my coworkers.
